task.title: Font resources and descriptors
task.shortdesc: Load your own fonts with the @font-face rule or with a fonts folder. Each rule names a family, lists the sources of one face and describes what the face provides, so that CSSMedia can choose it.

context.p: Use a fonts folder when you reuse the same fonts in many projects. Pass the folder with the -f option. CSSMedia reads the files with the extensions .ttf, .otf, .ttc and .otc in the folder and in its subfolders, and takes the family names from the fonts. Then you name a family in font-family, with no other declaration.
Use @font-face when you want to load a font from a file or a web address, or to give a font another family name:

The descriptors inside the rule describe a font face, not an element of your XML. Write one rule for each face of the family, such as the regular, bold and italic faces. Each rule needs a font-family and a src descriptor. CSSMedia ignores an invalid declaration, and when a descriptor occurs more than once in a rule, it uses the last valid value.

A family that you declare with @font-face hides an installed or standard family with the same name. When CSSMedia cannot load any source of a rule, it prints a warning and the family has no face from that rule.

step.cmd: Name the family and the sources

info.p: The font-family descriptor gives the name that the font-family property uses. It replaces the names that are stored in the font file. Write the name as a string, or as one or more identifiers.
The src descriptor is a comma-separated list of sources. CSSMedia tries them in order and uses the first that it can load:

ul.li: url() is the address of a font file. A relative address is resolved against the address of the stylesheet. It can be a file or a web address.
local() is the full name or the PostScript name of a face in the fonts folder. It does not name a family.

info.p: CSSMedia reads OpenType and TrueType fonts, font collections, and WOFF and WOFF 2.0 files. A url() value can end with a fragment that names the face to use from a collection, such as url("fonts.ttc#Example-Bold"). The fragment is the PostScript name of the face.
A url() source can have two hints. They let CSSMedia skip a source without loading it. Write format() first and then tech().

format() names the format of the file. CSSMedia supports collection, opentype, truetype, woff and woff2. It skips the sources with another format, such as embedded-opentype and svg. The strings "woff2", "woff", "truetype", "opentype" and "collection" are accepted as well. The strings that end in -variations, such as "woff2-variations", mean the format plus tech(variations).
tech() lists the technologies that the font needs, separated by commas. CSSMedia skips the source when it does not support one of them. It supports these:

ul.li: features-opentype and features-aat: layout features of OpenType and of Apple Advanced Typography.
variations and avar2: variable fonts and their axis remapping.
palettes, color-COLRv0, color-COLRv1, color-SVG, color-sbix and color-CBDT: color fonts.

info.p: The technologies features-graphite and incremental are not supported, so CSSMedia skips the sources that need them.

The descriptors font-weight, font-width and font-style tell CSSMedia which requests the face can satisfy. Their initial value is auto, which reads the information from the font. Write one value, or two values to state a range that a variable font covers:

ul.li: font-weight takes normal, bold or a number from 1 to 1000.

font-width takes a percentage or a width keyword. The keywords are 50%, 62.5%, 75%, 87.5%, 100%, 112.5%, 125%, 150% and 200%, from ultra-condensed to ultra-expanded. The old name font-stretch is an alias.
font-style takes normal, italic, left, right, or oblique with no angle, one angle or two angles from -90deg to 90deg.

info.p: The font-size descriptor limits the sizes for which the face is used. It takes one number, or two numbers for a range. The numbers are font sizes in CSS pixels, without a unit. Use it for fonts that have a face for each size, such as a text face and a display face.

The font-named-instance descriptor selects a named instance of a variable font, such as "Condensed Bold". The value is a string that CSSMedia compares with the names of the instances, without regard to case. If no instance has the name, the descriptor has no effect. The weight, width and style that you request are applied first, and the axes of the named instance replace them.

step.cmd: Limit the face to some characters

info.p: The unicode-range descriptor lists the characters for which the face can be used. The value is a comma-separated list of code points such as U+0041, ranges such as U+0400-04FF, and ranges with wildcards such as U+4??, where each ? stands for one hexadecimal digit. The initial value covers all characters:

Two rules with the same family and the same style make one family. CSSMedia uses the face of each character from the rules whose range includes it. If the ranges overlap, the rule that comes last wins. A range does not guarantee that the font has the glyph. If it does not, CSSMedia goes on with the next family of the list.

step.cmd: Set the defaults of the face

info.p: Three descriptors set what the face does by default. A property of the same name in your rules replaces the descriptor:

ul.li: font-feature-settings turns OpenType features on or off by their tags. Font variants and features explains the value.
font-variation-settings sets the axes of a variable font. Variable and color fonts explains the value. Use font-weight, font-width and font-style for the standard axes.
font-language-override sets the OpenType language system of the face, as Font variants and features explains.

step.cmd: Adjust the metrics of the face

info.p: Fonts of different families look different at the same size, and their lines have different heights. Adjust a face so that it fits with the others:

ul.li: size-adjust scales the glyphs and the metrics of the face by a percentage. The initial value is 100%. The font size does not change.

ascent-override, descent-override and line-gap-override replace the ascent, the descent and the line gap of the font. Each takes normal or a percentage of the font size. The first value is for horizontal text, and an optional second value is for vertical text.

superscript-position-override, superscript-size-override, subscript-position-override and subscript-size-override replace the position and the size of the glyphs that font-variant-position creates. Each takes normal, from-font or a percentage. The initial value is normal.
